metadata.title: Team Topologies: Organizing Business and Technology Teams for Fast Flow
metadata.abstract_summary: Skelton and Pais name and formalise "platform team" as one of four fundamental team types, and pair it with a specific discipline against over-building it — the "thinnest viable platform" — the closest thing organisational practice has to a named answer for this vault's own gap-analysis question about consolidating independent codebases onto shared infrastructure without merging them.

sections.heading: Claims
sections.text: The book's own framing, as published on the authors' website: a platform team is "a grouping of other team types that provide a compelling internal product to accelerate delivery by Stream-aligned teams," and its role is to "create services that accelerate stream-aligned teams, removing complexity." The companion constraint, in Skelton's own words explaining the thinnest viable platform (TVP): a platform "could be just a wiki page if that's all you need for your platform... you don't make it any thicker than necessary." The book presents four fundamental team types (stream-aligned, platform, enabling, complicated-subsystem) and three team interaction modes as its full toolkit; platform team is one of the four, not the whole model.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Not an empirical study: the book is a practice synthesis, drawing on the authors' consulting experience and prior published team-topology and DevOps-topology work (Skelton's earlier "DevOps topologies" material predates the book) rather than a controlled comparison. The TVP concept is presented illustratively — through examples of platforms that stayed too thin versus organisations that over-built — rather than through a measured study.

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
This note is built from the authors' own first-party web content — `teamtopologies.com/key-concepts` and the linked `what-is-a-thinnest-viable-platform-tvp` page, both credited to Skelton and Pais and published by their own organisation — plus confirmed bibliographic metadata for the book itself (title, authors, publisher IT Revolution Press, ISBN 9781942788812, first published 7 September 2019; a second edition followed in 2025). **The book's full text was not read for this note.** What is recorded here is grounded in what was actually read: the authors' own summary pages, not the book's complete argument, evidence base, or case studies. Treat the Claim and Relevance sections as reliable for what the authors assert the concept to be; treat this note as a pointer to the book for anyone who needs its full supporting argument, not a substitute for reading it.

The concept itself is also, by its nature, prescriptive rather than measured — "keep it thin" is a design heuristic the authors recommend, not a finding with a reported effect size or a named failure-rate reduction.
